name: Sentence Length Variance
description: Measures the statistical dispersion of sentence lengths around the document's mean. Large Language Models naturally converge toward a mathematical average, producing sentences that are consistently similar in length (e.g., 18 words, 20 words, 17 words). This creates a rhythmic monotony. Human writers naturally exhibit high sentence length variance, effortlessly juxtaposing a punchy 3-word declarative sentence right next to a sprawling 45-word explanatory sentence to maintain reader engagement and emphasize key points.
mechanism: The system calculates the word count for every sentence to find the document's mean sentence length ($\mu$) and the standard deviation ($\sigma$). The Coefficient of Variation (CV) normalizes this data, measuring how much individual sentence lengths vary relative to the average. A low CV score mathematically proves that the text is rhythmically homogenized and artificially generated. A high CV score indicates organic, human-like pacing with significant structural diversity.
useCase: Highly effective for auditing cover letters, marketing copy, and essays where a monotonous rhythm is the most glaring 'tell' of AI authorship.
strengths:
• Extremely difficult for AI models to naturally replicate without sounding disjointed; prompting an AI to 'vary sentence lengths' often results in awkward, forced transitions rather than natural human flow.
• Completely language and topic agnostic, relying purely on the mathematical distribution of spaces/words.
limitations:
• Requires a minimum of 8-10 sentences to calculate a statistically meaningful variance.
• Deliberately rigid human writing, such as highly formal technical specifications or strict legal clauses, will naturally exhibit low variance and may trigger a false positive.
parameters:
Analysis: Word Count Isolation per Sentence
Metric: Coefficient of Variation (Standard Deviation normalized by Mean)
Output: 0-100 Rhythmic Rigidity (Mathematical Monotony) Score
accuracy: High — 80-87% accuracy. One of the most reliable and computationally lightweight statistical fingerprints of algorithmic text generation.

references.title: Uchendu, A. et al. (2020). Authorship Attribution for Neural Text Generation. EMNLP.
Ippolito, D. et al. (2020). Automatic Detection of Generated Text is Easiest when Humans are Fooled. ACL.
